spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players using 146,028 player-referee dyads across four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) in the 2012-2013 season
the hypothesis that referees are biased against dark-skinned players is supported
the model adjusted for position, league, playing style, physical characteristics, and referee country bias
dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players after adjustment
adjusted risk difference is 0.236 percentage points (95% CI [0.022, 0.451] pp; p=0.031)
adjusted odds ratio is 1.203 (95% CI [1.026, 1.409]; p=0.023)
dark-skinned players are approximately 19% more likely to receive red cards relative to the baseline rate
adjusted risk difference restated as 0.236pp with 95% CI [0.022,0.451]pp and two-sided p=0.0309
probability of a red card is 0.236pp higher for dark-skinned (1.41%) than light-skinned (1.22%) players after adjustment
this difference represents a 19.4% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline rate
three estimation approaches were used to check robustness of the risk-difference estimate
the primary approach used a linear probability model with HC3 robust standard errors
this approach yielded RD=0.236pp (95% CI [0.022,0.451]pp), p=0.031
an alternative approach used a linear probability model with player-clustered standard errors
this approach yielded RD=0.236pp (95% CI [-0.009,0.481]pp), p=0.059, not statistically significant
a further alternative used logistic regression average marginal effects
this approach yielded RD=0.221pp (95% CI [0.031,0.411]pp), p=0.023
all three approaches yield highly consistent point estimates (~0.22-0.24 pp)
HC3 robust standard errors were preferred as the more conservative choice, accounting for heteroskedasticity without clustering assumptions
adjusted odds ratio is 1.203 (95% CI [1.026,1.409]), two-sided p=0.0225
odds of a red card are 20.3% higher for dark-skinned players, holding other factors constant
this odds ratio is statistically significant at the 0.05 level
the unadjusted odds ratio was 1.163 (95% CI [1.005,1.345]; p=0.042)
adjustment for confounders slightly strengthened the association compared to the unadjusted estimate
the unit of analysis chosen was player-referee dyads (N=99,535 in complete-case analysis)
each observation aggregates the interaction history between a specific player and referee across all their matches
the outcome is defined as whether the dyad had any red card(s) across all encounters
total dyads = 99,535
unique players = 1,214 (1,015 light-skinned, 199 dark-skinned)
unique referees = 2,758
referee countries = 161
light-skinned dyads = 83,582, with 1,016 red cards (rate 1.22%)
dark-skinned dyads = 15,953, with 225 red cards (rate 1.41%)
two independent raters, blind to the research question, categorized players on a 5-point scale from player photos
the rating scale ran from 0.00 (very light) to 1.00 (very dark) in 0.25 increments
exact rater agreement was 76.8%
agreement within 0.25 points was 99.9%
Spearman correlation between raters was 0.858
light skin was defined as average rating 0.00-0.325
dark skin was defined as average rating 0.675-1.00
medium skin (average rating 0.326-0.674) was excluded from the primary analysis to create a clearer contrast
the analysis controlled for factors that could confound the skin tone/red card relationship
player position (12 named categories) was adjusted for as a covariate, since position affects card risk and skin-tone distribution varies by position
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) was adjusted for as a covariate
dark-skinned player representation varies by league: France 35%, England 21%, Germany 9%, Spain 9%
number of games in the dyad was adjusted for as a continuous covariate
yellow cards in the dyad was adjusted for as a continuous covariate, as a proxy for aggressive playing style
goals scored in the dyad was adjusted for as a continuous covariate, as an indicator of playing style
player height (cm) was adjusted for as a continuous covariate
player weight (kg) was adjusted for as a continuous covariate
referee-country implicit bias (meanIAT, from Project Implicit) was adjusted for as a continuous covariate
referee-country explicit bias (meanExp, racial thermometer task) was adjusted for as a continuous covariate
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original dataset) were excluded due to missing/unavailable player photos
17,015 dyads (13.7% of those with ratings) with medium skin tones were excluded
8,071 dyads (7.5% of the light/dark comparison) were excluded for missing covariates: position (6.9%), weight (0.6%), height (0.04%), or bias measures (0.1%)
the final analysis sample is 99,535 dyads (68.2% of the original dataset)
the primary analysis used a linear probability model estimated via OLS
the outcome was coded as a binary indicator of any red card in the dyad
the exposure was coded as a binary indicator of dark skin
robust standard errors used were HC3 heteroskedasticity-consistent (preferred) or player-clustered (alternative)
secondary analysis used logistic regression to estimate odds ratios
average marginal effects were computed to provide an alternative risk-difference estimate
three standard-error estimation approaches were tested for robustness
HC3 robust SE was preferred as the most conservative, accounting for heteroskedasticity
player-clustered SE was used to account for multiple dyads per player
standard logistic regression was used for odds-ratio inference
all three standard-error approaches yielded consistent inferences, supporting robustness of the findings
skin-tone ratings were averaged across the two raters
the averaged rating was then categorized into a light/dark binary variable
the red-card outcome was coded as any red card (>0) vs none (0) in the dyad
continuous predictors were used in their original scale; no transformations were applied
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported by the data
the adjusted risk difference of 0.236pp is statistically significant (p=0.031, two-sided)
the 95% CI [0.022,0.451]pp excludes zero
the effect is robust across multiple estimation approaches and standard-error specifications
the adjusted odds ratio of 1.203 (95% CI [1.026,1.409]) confirms a meaningful increase in red-card odds
a sensitivity analysis addressing playing-style factors (yellow cards, goals) was conducted (text appears garbled/truncated in source)
physical characteristics (height, weight) were addressed as part of this evidence/sensitivity list
league differences were addressed as part of this evidence/sensitivity list
exposure (number of games) was addressed as part of this evidence/sensitivity list
referee-country racial bias measures were addressed as part of this evidence/sensitivity list
the study used an observational design rather than a randomized experiment, controlling for many potential confounders

the analysis could not control for individual player aggression/temperament, quality of play/skill level, team tactics/coaching, match importance/context, or referee characteristics beyond country-level bias measures

spans.note: caveats that photo-based ratings may not reflect real-time perception, that the dichotomization may not capture racial-perception complexity, and that raters differ from referees' in-person perception

spans.assertion: inter-rater agreement (77% exact, though highly correlated) indicates some measurement error

spans.note: players without photos may differ systematically; restriction to four leagues/one season leaves generalizability uncertain

spans.assertion: only male professional players were included in the analysis

spans.note: dyad-level aggregation across matches could mask within-dyad heterogeneity

spans.assertion: two-way clustering by player and referee would have been more appropriate than the methods used, but was not implemented because it was computationally challenging
the HC3 robust SE approach used does not explicitly account for clustering
red cards occur in only ~1.2% of dyads, limiting statistical power

spans.note: LPM can in principle predict outside [0,1], considered unlikely given the low baseline rate

spans.assertion: logistic regression (considered more appropriate for rare outcomes) yielded results consistent with the LPM

spans.note: running several specifications/sensitivity analyses increases Type I error risk

spans.assertion: findings were consistent across approaches, suggesting robustness rather than spurious significance

spans.note: yellow cards/goals/playing style could be mediators rather than confounders; controlling for them may underestimate the total effect
referee country-level bias measures may not reflect individual referee attitudes

spans.assertion: the aggregate bias measures show limited within-country variation

spans.note: excluding medium-skin-tone dyads limits ability to assess dose-response relationships

spans.assertion: a sensitivity analysis using continuous skin tone (rather than the binary categorization) was conducted
the continuous-skin-tone analysis showed results consistent with the main findings, mitigating the exclusion concern

spans.note: LPM assumes constant treatment effects and linear relationships, and could predict probabilities outside [0,1]

spans.assertion: logistic regression with average marginal effects gave consistent estimates, alleviating the LPM-assumption concern
analyzing skin tone as continuous (all categories, N=115,457 dyads) gave an odds ratio per unit increase of 1.269 (95% CI [1.049,1.534], p=0.014)
this suggests a dose-response relationship, with darker skin tones associated with progressively higher red-card probabilities
exploratory analysis found the effect of skin tone on red cards varies significantly across leagues
in England, the association is positive (baseline reference)
in France, the association is negative or null (significant negative interaction, p<0.001)
in Germany, the effect is similar to England with no significant interaction
in Spain, the association is weaker/positive (significant negative interaction, p=0.040)
the heterogeneity suggests the magnitude of bias may depend on league context, referee training, or player demographics
the overall positive effect is driven primarily by England and Germany
the unadjusted risk difference (0.195pp) was slightly smaller than the adjusted estimate (0.236pp), indicating confounders partially mask the true association
dark-skinned players' characteristics (e.g., playing more in France, certain positions) would typically reduce red-card risk, making the adjusted effect more pronounced once accounted for

spans.note: recommendations for future research (causal designs, match-level analysis, video coding, referee demographics, temporal trends, other outcomes, mediation analysis, replication)
